hook: Nick Bostrom is a Swedish philosopher who has shaped how both academics and the public think about the long term risks and possibilities of advanced technology. He trained across physics, computational neuroscience, and philosophy at the universities of Gothenburg, Stockholm, and King's College London, and completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000. In 2002 he published the paper Existential Risks, which introduced a systematic taxonomy of the ways humanity's long term potential could be destroyed or permanently curtailed. In 2005 he founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, building it from three researchers into a center that helped incubate the fields of AI safety and effective altruism before it closed in 2024. His 2014 book Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies became a New York Times bestseller and is widely credited with moving concerns about advanced AI from niche discussion into mainstream academic and public debate. He continues this work as founder of the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia in 2024.

quote.text: Machine intelligence is the last invention that humanity will ever need to make.
quote.context: From his TED talk, What happens when our computers get smarter than we are?, March 2015

moniker: Philosopher of existential risk and superintelligence

timeline.event: Completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics after earlier studies in philosophy, mathematics, physics, and computational neuroscience.
timeline.impact: Built the unusually broad, cross disciplinary base that shaped his later work on existential risk.

timeline.event: Published Existential Risks, Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios and Related Hazards in the Journal of Evolution and Technology.
timeline.impact: Introduced a systematic taxonomy of existential risk into academic philosophy.

timeline.event: Founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University.
timeline.impact: Built one of the first academic research centers dedicated to existential risk, growing it to roughly 50 researchers before it closed in 2024.

timeline.event: Co-edited the volume Global Catastrophic Risks with Milan Cirkovic.
timeline.impact: Produced an early comprehensive scholarly survey of catastrophic and existential risks.
Became a New York Times bestseller that brought AI existential risk into mainstream academic and public discourse.

timeline.event: Closed the Future of Humanity Institute, founded the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia.
timeline.impact: Continued his research program on humanity's long term future outside the university system.

quick_facts: Holds degrees in philosophy, physics, mathematical logic, and computational neuroscience from four different universities
Completed his PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000
Founded and directed Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute from 2005 until its closure in 2024
His book Superintelligence became a New York Times bestseller
Named twice to Foreign Policy's list of Top 100 Global Thinkers

achievements.title: Founding the Future of Humanity Institute
achievements.impact: Built an academic hub for existential risk research that helped incubate the AI safety and effective altruism movements.

achievements.title: Existential Risks (2002)
achievements.impact: Gave researchers a shared vocabulary and taxonomy for thinking about threats to humanity's long term survival.

achievements.title: Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014)
achievements.impact: Moved concerns about advanced AI from a niche topic into mainstream academic and public debate, drawing public engagement from figures such as Bill Gates and Elon Musk.

achievements.title: The simulation argument
achievements.impact: Produced one of the most widely discussed philosophical arguments of the last two decades about the probability that we live in a computer simulation.
